lesson_title: Salt Water In, Three Industries Out: Electrolysis
hook_text: The most valuable dirt on Earth falls off a copper slab in a refinery tank. It's full of gold.
clip_script: A galvanic cell is chemistry rolling downhill — it pays you. Electrolysis is the opposite: you pay chemistry to run uphill, and the products are worth every cent. Exhibit one: your phone charging tonight. The wall socket forces the battery's reaction backwards, rebuilding chemicals so they can fall again tomorrow. Galvanic all day, electrolytic all night. Exhibit two: the refinery. A slab of impure copper dissolves at the positive electrode while perfect copper rains onto the negative one — and the gold, silver and platinum trapped in the slab refuse to dissolve at the tuned voltage. They just drop. The sludge on the tank floor is the most valuable dirt on Earth, and selling it helps pay for the electricity. Exhibit three: salt water. Force a current through concentrated brine and one cheap input becomes three industries — chlorine gas for clean drinking water and PVC pipes, hydrogen for fuel, and caustic soda for every bar of soap you have ever used. The twist? Sodium ions queue at the electrode and get refused — water outbids them, so hydrogen bubbles out and sodium metal never appears. Electrodes are auctions, not queues. Uphill chemistry, purchased at the socket — and it built half the objects in your house.
visual_style: Energy flowing uphill against a hill silhouette; a dirty copper slab shedding golden grains into glittering sludge; a tank of brine splitting into three labelled product streams — pool water, fuel, soap.
mood: Industrial wonder — the economy of forced chemistry, told as three exhibits.
pacing: Downhill-versus-uphill setup, three quick exhibits with a beat each, auction twist, sweeping close.
